utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We heard testimony here from a witness of Mr. Nice's, Beqe Beqaj. He testified on the 29th of August, 2002, and the transcript is somewhere from line or page 9116 to 9120. It's in that part of the transcript where you'll find that passage. He was talking about the fact that in August 1998, the population of Racak and other villages left the village for the first time when the army and the police arrived in both villages and other surrounding villages in the valley. And on the 14th of August, 1999, he says the army of Yugoslavia MUP again arrived to the village of Raca, and the witness says that they ordered the villagers to leave their homes. Also, that on the 27th of April, five Serb policemen were killed after which the Serb forces attacked the village of Dobrosh where a number of villagers were killed, and the inhabitants fled from the village in the direction of Meja where the Serb forces stopped the convoy at a checkpoint in Meja and then separated 24 men that they sent to the fields as -- which was known as Hasan's valley. They separated 30 of them there, and the policemen said that they were responsible for the killing of the Serb policemen, and the witness says that he never saw them again. Tell me if you know anything about that and what all this was about. I hope that you paid attention to the dates, the 27th of April when five of our policemen were killed, and then it says our forces attacked the village of Dobrosh.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: They separated 13 of them, not 30.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you mention 1998, the witness probably made a mistake in stating the date because when dealing with 1998 ourselves, we had some orders linked to the return of the population to those villages. That means that the inhabitants, in 1998, could have left in the month of May, whereas in August when the witness and the witnesses mentioning August, they were already back in their homes. Now, as far as 1999 is concerned, this particular date, the 27th of April that you mentioned, I said yesterday already or, rather, I indicated on the map that on the 27th of April, the operations started in that region and that the object of those operations was to break the terrorist forces which had gathered in the immediate vicinity of the state border. That is to say they are the villages that I pointed to yesterday beginning with Smonica towards Junik. So it's a broader territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, General, but what I'm asking you now is this: What this witness stated, that some men were separated and then nothing is known of their fate after that, is that true?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the separation of men goes, it was often usual that the terrorists together with the civilians, that they should mingle with the civilians, take off their uniforms, because they were wearing civilian clothing and uniforms. They'd just discard their uniforms and become civilians straight away. So the police or, rather, the army couldn't do that. The army didn't have that kind of information. So the police would sometimes stop certain individuals to search them and to see if they were indeed civilians or not. Otherwise, I don't know anything about that. The killing of some policemen was mentioned. All I know is that during those days four policemen were killed, in fact, and that one policeman was seriously wounded and that he remained an invalid after that wounding. That's what I know linked to that particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was it at all possible for somebody to set aside, to separate these individuals, to search them, check them out, anybody, and then to kill them? So to separate them, single them out, and kill them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When people are singled out, separated, and in 1998 I was present when that was -- that situation took place, when you separate a group of people, what you do is you look for their names. You can't do that on the spot. You can't check them out on the spot, but you have to ring up headquarters, then you give the person's name, then this is checked through the computer. You do a computer process check on them for the individuals and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is is it possible that some killing could have taken place in that procedure, that checking procedure that you mention now?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during that procedure that is quite impossible because, had something like that happened, it would have been a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're not contesting that, but do you know that anything like that happened?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about anything like that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Now, Nike Peraj, a Prosecution witness, said that at the beginning of 1999 that the Serb artillery and army deployed in the Djakovica municipality, Pec, Prizren and Orahovica, that they were there, and he testified from the 9th to the 13th of May, 2002 and that is mentioned in this fillbox of Mr. Nice's.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and the witness, there is a request from the interpreter for you to both slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested, General, since these are large towns, or relatively large towns, not to categorise towns and the size of them, Djakovica, Pec, Prizren and Orahovac, he says that in 1999, the Serb artillery and the army, without going into what he means by artillery and what he means by army, but he says the artillery and army were deployed in the Djakovica. Pec, Prizren, Orahovac municipalities and towns. Now in those towns, were there any Yugoslav army garrisons located there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pec there was a garrison, yes, in which there were several units of the rank of a battalion, strength of battalion. In Djakovica, there were two barracks, a garrison with two barracks, that is. In one of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the barracks there was the Border Battalion and my own 2nd Motorised Battalion, and in the other barracks there was the entire brigade put up with five divisions, the PVO Brigade, and the command and all the units of the brigade and the border battalions, as well as the command of the military district of Prizren, which means -- which means that no units were deployed, and they were always there in that garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's where the barracks exist?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's where the barracks exist, and they have existed there since World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. He said that in April 1999, the KLA killed Milutin Prascevic, who was the chief of the MUP in Djakovica, as well as four other policemen, after which, on the 27th, 28th of April, there was a large-scale operation in the valley north of Djakovica. He talks about Serb forces, and he testified from the 9th to the 13th of May, and I've already told you that, 2002. What was happening? What happened? So we're talking about April 1999, the 27th and 28th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those observations by this witness, there is -- there are untruths. I knew this man Milutin Prascevic. He wasn't the chief of MUP at all. He could have been just a lower-ranking officer in the MUP of Djakovica, and I've already said that four policemen were killed, one among them was an Albanian, and one was seriously wounded. However, those policemen, when they were called by some Roma, as far as I was informed, some Roma called them up and they went out in the direction of Ponosevac and Smonica to intervene and that's where four of them were killed and one seriously wounded. But to bring that into connection, that is to say the death of those policemen and this activity on this other territory has nothing to do with one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the activity you've explained to us, that is to say the defence of the border and the onslaught from -- coming from Albania, the attack from Albania --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the greatest amount of fighting during the war. 120 of our soldiers were killed in defending our borders, and these were supposed to be forces which would hit from the rear to join up with the forces attacking from Albania, this other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's not dwell on that any longer, then. The witness Xhevahire Syla said here -- she said here that on the 14th of April, the Serb forces entered Novokaz, Djakovica municipality -- or Djakovo municipality and they went into Albania houses, giving the people, the inhabitants five minutes to leave, and this led to the formation of a convoy moving to Djakovica, and that the police attacked the people in the convoy, told them to go to Albania, and that the refugees were not allowed to leave the route they had taken towards Prizren and which was a circuitous route to the border, a roundabout way, and it says that the convoy was stopped at the Bistrazin bridge, that the Serb forces separated from -- the people from the convoy, that the convoy was later hit by NATO bombs, and then three low-flying planes later on, carrying Serb flags, flew over their heads and bombed the convoy seven times, killing 70 to 80 persons. And she testified on the 17th of July, 2002 and the transcript is 8186, that page of the transcript. I hope that you listened to what I read out and said carefully; so the NATO bombing, then our planes bombing and then killing 70, 80 people. That's what she claimed.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite nonsensical, ludicrous, because NATO -- on the first day NATO didn't recognise this, but they did admit to it on the second or third day, of having bombed on the 14th of April columns of refugees, but not only in that area that the witness is referring to. The refugees were bombed on -- in some five or six separate positions from the place that the witness mentions, that is from Bistrazin right up to Prizren, and a large number of civilians were killed as a result and especially large number wounded. And there is footage, there is a film of that, film by state television, and I also think that foreign journalists were later on able to come to the spot and film the column the next day. But first of all there was this state television footage, and it's quite nonsensical that NATO planes bombed first and that our planes appeared later on. Our planes absolutely never flew, did not fly at all from the end of March. They were not airborne from the end of March to the end the war. Our planes never took off during that period of time because they were inferior, because they were not able to stand up to NATO planes, NATO aviation, that had complete supremacy over the airspace of our country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did your planes also bomb? Generally speaking, not speaking about in relation to that particular incident. During the conflict, did your planes drop bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you should know first of all the kind of air force that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had. So as far as fighter planes go, it only had 12 planes, MiG-29, the MiG-29 type that were located in Belgrade, the -- a MiG-, which just before the war was supposed to be overhauled, and seven of those 12 planes were destroyed in the vicinity of Belgrade; Belgrade, Valjevo, in that general area. As to the other planes -- and that was all in March. As to the other planes, they were no longer flying. Now, the other planes we had were the MiG-21, and that is the second generation of aeroplanes which had absolutely no chance against the aeroplanes of the fourth generation which NATO had in its possession. And then there was a third plane, a third aeroplane in our possession. It was the Orao, or eagle plane, which is a light plane for combat operations with very limited capabilities, and it was a support plane, as we call it, for support operations. However, as those planes had absolutely no chance against the other side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, never mind that. What is the answer to the question that I asked? You have this habit of not answering a question. You go off on your own tangent. I asked you whether your planes dropped bombs. Were they equipped to drop bombs? If they were not equipped to drop bombs, then that would settle it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our aircraft never bombed a single target during the war. You are now asking me if they were equipped to do so. Of course they were equipped to do so, but only if there had been no NATO supremacy in the airspace. Since NATO had supremacy in the airspace, they could make no sorties in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that your low flying planes dropped bombs on the convoy, and you're saying that didn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. happen. What is the basis for saying that didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I'm a military man. I know my army. Although I'm a soldier of the ground forces, I also know the aviation and to some extent its tactics, and at the end of the day I know when our planes made sorties. NATO did admit to bombing this column of refugees. What the witness is saying is pure nonsense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say NATO admitted to this bombing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have evidence of this, this admission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a well-known commentator of the NATO, Jamie Shea. He was their spokesperson. I don't have this evidence with me, I didn't know I would need it, because the entire world knows that NATO bombed both this column of refugees and another column of refugees a month later in Korishte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Another witness, Merfidete Selmani stated on the 16th of July, 2002, that on the 14th of April - that is on the same day - Serb soldiers entered the village of Dobros, making the villagers flee, and when they passed Djakovica and came near the Bistrazin bridge the witness heard an explosion and heard or, rather, saw smoke coming from a part of the convoy. There were corpses around. A tractor was hit, et cetera. Does this relate to the same event or something else?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there on the spot after it happened. What the witness is talking about I saw with my own eyes. I saw the corpses. I saw assistance being given in my military hospital after the incident, to the wounded. From Bistrazin all the way to Prizren, the convoy was hit by many bombs. There were many dead. There were many destroyed vehicles. There were many dead people, people who were completely incinerated on their tractor trailers. It was a very terrible sight to see. We managed to lend some assistance to the wounded. We transferred some of them to the hospital in Djakovica, some to Prizren. They were taken care of there. There were many serious wounds and many amputations of limbs. That is the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are many witnesses who claim that it was our forces who did that, and it's very important to emphasise this here.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a recording of the communication between NATO pilots. We have it in our country. It has been published. One of the NATO pilots, after receiving command to attack, says that he only sees tractors on the road, he only sees red tractors, because all the tractors produced in our country are red. But he received a command to attack. So that was an attack on civilians, pure and simple. If the Court needs this evidence, I can provide a transcript of this communication. It has been published in our press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, General. Another witness of Mr. Nice's, Martin Pnishi, who testified on the 29th of August, 2002, transcript 9216 and 17, says that on the 27th of April, around 9.30, he saw from his house that Serb forces had set up a checkpoint about 200 metres from his house in Meja. The checkpoint was set up by the army, police officers, and armoured vehicles. What happened in Meja on the 27th of April, 1999? Do you have any knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have as much knowledge as I received from my subordinate commanders' reports. I knew that this operation against terrorists was being carried out in this area, and I knew that my unit or, rather, part of the unit that had already been there defending the state border was allocated in order to block the road about a kilometre from Meja towards Ponosevac to prevent the overflow or withdrawal of terrorist forces. Over those few days in the written reports of my subordinate commander, I saw that his units were blocking, in blocking position, and that from one column fire was opened at his unit and two of his soldiers wounded plus another soldier the next day, and I have reports concerning this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I already opened my binder while we were dealing with these witnesses to deal with your document 438. It's a command to support MUP forces in crushing and destroying Siptar terrorist forces in Malisevo sector, strictly confidential, 455-90. What is the substance of this order under your tab 438?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the completion of operations in this area, Orahovac, Suva Reka, Pirane, Krusa, and so on, upon orders of the corps command, operations were moved to the other side of Malisevac Mountain towards Krusevo because there was a larger concentration of terrorist forces there. The map under 439 goes together with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. The map is under the next tab. Does it indicate everything that should, according to the order, be included in the disposition of your forces?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the decision to crush Siptar terrorist forces in the Malisevo sector, and it says an excerpt for the 549th Brigade. This is just an excerpt showing the assignment for my brigade and the neighbouring units, 243rd Brigade and 15th Brigade. In this order we see information about terrorist forces, where they are located, their strength. Then we see the assignment of the corps, the decision of the commander, and towards the end, assignments of particular units. As far as my unit is concerned, my assignment was to support MUP forces from this axis here where operations had been carried out earlier on the 27th combat group 5, which near Dobrodeljane village acted towards the north was now acting together with the others, across Mount Milanovac to crush terrorist forces located here on the slopes of Mount Milanovac and to use part of the forces to go area of Orahovac-Ostrozub-Dragobilje road, and to act from the flank to support forces and act in coordination with them in their attack from the direction of Suva Reka. And you see the axes of operation on this map. In the Dragobilje area, the terrorist headquarters were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the first page we even have an enumeration of these forces: 122nd KLA Brigade, around 300 terrorists; 115th Brigade, around 250 men; 116th KLA Brigade, around 250 men; and the Gani Pacarizi KLA Brigade, there is no strength indicated, but that makes four brigades active in this area.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the information we had at the time about those Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, under para 9, let me quote just the last line. Does it say here: "In all situations, consistently comply with the provisions of the international laws of war"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is under paragraph 9, Morale and Psychological Support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says in another paragraph: "Escort captured terrorists to the prison for prisoners of war and prohibit members of units from entering villages, from looting, from entering enemy headquarters and bases prior to the arrival of expert teams."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We had -- we have already dealt with the map. Now under tab 440 -- my copy is very bad.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my order for the same operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, the map we just saw before, the map on the easel, was it drawn at that time or drawn at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that was a contemporaneous map, a map from that time. This is a copy, a section of the main map, and it says here "Section or excerpt for the 549th Motorised Brigade." That is my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. General, under tab 441, we see your decision, that is a map indicating your decision. It says "Decision of the commander of the 549th Brigade for crushing and destroying Siptar terrorist forces in Malisevo sector." This map is signed by you. In the upper left corner, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Approved by Commander General Lazarevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's the same technology that you described in your earlier answers: You receive an order, then you prepare your own order, your decision is shown on the map, the map is then approved by your superior commander, head of the Pristina Corps. Is that the same technology that is repeated on a day-to-day basis in operations on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I receive a map and an order, and then I develop my own map and my own order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you get an order and a map from the corps level and then you make your own map and order.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then, as you described in your previous analysis of earlier operations, after each and every completed assignment you prepare an analysis. Do we see under tab 442 your analysis of what we have just seen? The order, the map, your map, your order, and then your analysis?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a complete analysis of this operation. A very detailed analysis of all the activities of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It relies upon the same order, 455-90, of the 28th. Could you please point out the main elements of this analysis. Let me just emphasise the estimates towards the end of the first page, where you say: "We estimate that the Siptar terrorist forces suffered the following losses: Around 70 dead." In the previous operation, your estimation was 85 dead. Here it's 70 members of the KLA killed. That's your estimate for this operation.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in Pagarusa area, which is just behind the first lines, we found 30 terrorists buried. That is our estimate of their losses. What is characteristic of this operation? Particularly on this axis leading from Suva Reka, that is a part of the territory which we never, in 1998 or 1999, entered. That is a well-fortified mountainous terrain. It's called a multi-storey defence. From this area towards Pagarusa our forces were unable to advance for several days, not even a step forward. All the forces coming from Orahovac via Ostrozub and via Milanovic village managed to hit the flank and the rear of the forces that were defending themselves from the direction of Suva Reka. And only then did the defence of the terrorists weaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In conclusion, you say: "The assignment set to the unit was successfully implemented. Terrorist forces were successfully crushed and control was established over the territory, in particular over the Pagarusa sector, for the first time since the start of the armed rebellion of last year. Units of the 549th Motorised Brigade and MUP forces have now been relieved from the provocations in this area. They are relieved from the pressure by the Siptar terrorist forces on the town of Suva Reka and Orahovac. While we were carrying out the given assignment, forces of the NATO aggressor air force continuously performed reconnaissance flights and on some occasions attacked our forces with no negative consequences for them."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the analysis of this particular operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, in relation to what I've quoted from the order, in tab 443 you have your own order?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which pertains to implementation of international law of war and the army of Yugoslavia. And then you say: "I hereby order: Apply international humanitarian law," et cetera, et cetera, "against persons violating international humanitarian law, to sentence them to lawfully prescribed sanctions." You particularly prohibit unorganised entry into villages and any kind of arbitrary behaviour. Is that your order, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my order which was written on the basis of the order received from the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We've seen that already, we've dealt with that earlier on. And we have here in tab 445 the order of the 30th of March of General Lazarevic, Commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He also says, inter alia -- he says: "With a view to protecting the population leaving the jeopardised areas --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, stop. Let us know where exactly you're reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it is tab 444, not 445. Could you check it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said 444, or at least I think I said 444.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said 445.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. I opened 444, and I probably read the next Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tab number, although it is actually a document with the previous number. So it's a technical error. 444 is the number.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the commander of the Pristina Corps on measures to protect the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Regarding the entire population leaving the threatened areas, they should have unhindered passage towards the Republic of Albania and the Republic of Macedonia. "Secondly, use command measures to protect the population from improper conduct of individuals and groups and enable their free passage in the direction they choose. In dealing with the population, fully comply with international law of war and the provisions of the Geneva Conventions." Paragraph 3: "The responsible officers have the duty to start proceedings against persons violating the provisions of the international law of war, to sentence them to lawfully prescribed sanctions." Now, I assume and I'm going to ask you to give an explanation: "The population leaving the threatened areas in convoys in motor vehicles or on foot shall be directed along the routes leading towards the Republic of Albania and the Republic of Macedonia and any improper conduct towards it shall be prohibited." You explained in one of your answers, since some witnesses referred to this too, completely free, unhindered passage is referred to here whereas you talked about some parts of the territory that were mined, that there were mines along roads, et cetera. Why was it necessary to indicate the exact direction in which people were supposed to move in relation to what this order of General Lazarevic's also says?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, primarily this meant assist the population so that they would know where they could move safely. In my area, there were only three -- two directions or, rather, two border crossings; Cafa Prusit and Vrbnica. For four or five days the population was leaving through Cafa Prusit and they could only leave on foot. This is very difficult terrain to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please explain now since it was said here, not once, mind you, that they had to leave their vehicles and then walk all the way to the border. Why did they leave their vehicles and walk all the way to the border?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this direction everything was mined. There were anti-tank mines and anti-personnel mines. Cafa Pruse makes it possible to use armour, so all the way up to the village of Zup, that's about two or three kilometres in depth, there were minefields. So up to the village of Zup it was possible to ride on a motor vehicle, and from Zup there was only a single path going through the minefields, and we used it at that time, but it was so narrow you could only walk on foot. Therefore, those who wanted to walk went that way on foot, or they took motor vehicles via Prizren and then crossed into Albania through Vrbnica. Some witnesses say that here, and it is considered that the army assisted the civilians when they were leaving. Really here by Cafa Pruse the army was helping them, but in the following sense: Women, children, and the elderly were helped. They were brought through the border post of Zulfaj closer to the Cafa Prusit border crossing and they helped them negotiate the minefield and finally leave the territory of the country and go to a safe area. This has to do with transporting only women, children, or persons who were weak and taking the road via Zulfaj, going all the way around, because that was a better way of getting to the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that but I'm going back to the order now. It says here the population leaving the threatened area in convoys should be provided free passage in the direction they choose. That is to say they should be protected and enabled free passage in the direction they choose. Does that mean that you are not allowed to stop the population, to prevent them from leaving the war zones? Rather, you're supposed to help them leave where they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... material to the indictment, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I don't think this is of marginal importance, because persecutions are referred to all the time and it is due to persecutions that the population was leaving the area, and obviously the territory is being left by the population --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice was in fact suggesting that it is an issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm quoting the order. I'm quoting a document. If that is leading, quoting an order, then probably my question is leading too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, had you not taken these measures, could the population go through this area at all?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population would have suffered terrible losses in the minefields had we not followed them, escorted them. After the first day, we had certain ribbons and small poles marking the path through which they could move safely. So our task was to prevent the population from suffering any losses due to the fact that our minefields were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since both of these routes were mined, you explained that a bit earlier on, you said that you were expecting an armoured attack -- an attack on armoured vehicles coming from Albania and that that is why the minefields were there. Was anybody hurt or killed there in spite of the minefields?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Cafa Prusit there weren't any casualties, but there was only one in Vrbnica. Perhaps 20 metres from the border itself. One vehicle, a Lada vehicle, went out because only the right lane of the road had been de-mined. Due to some lack of discipline he was trying to overtake a vehicle in front of him and went to the left side therefor. The vehicle was destroyed. The persons in that vehicle were seriously injured and immediately transported to Albania. At one of these places, two policemen who were also not strictly abiding by the signs by the road, they came on the left lane and they wanted to turn around from Vrbnica to go back to Prizren, and they got off on a small byroad and were both killed by an anti-tank mine that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those are the only two incidents that occurred in your zone of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. responsibility. All the rest you secured properly so that everyone had safe passage.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as mining is concerned, those are the only incidents that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In tab 445 there is an order of commander Krsman Jelic that pertains to the rules of international law of war and the army of Yugoslavia. What kind of order is this?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is an order of mine, too, but you couldn't read it well. It's also the 549th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again this is based on the order of the commander of the Pristina Corps. Again this is a warning to commanders how to act in terms of observing the provisions of international laws of war and humanitarian law. In particular, there is a warning because in the field there were already many explosive devices that were thrown from NATO aircraft, and there is a ban on walking up to these explosive devices at all. They were supposed to be reported only and it was only experts who were supposed to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot deal with this because it's a totally illegible copy. I hope you have a more legible copy. And you yourself this is your own order?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's my own order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 is act in accordance with the international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chapter VII on the wounded and sick, and chapter VIII on the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there's also reference to 1998, the document from 1998 that remains important. So what do you say here? Who is responsible to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders of combat groups and the leaders of all units, as well as the commander of every brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say here in paragraph 3, as far as I can see, that against all persons violating the rules of international law on war --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- proceedings shall be started immediately.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what else?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On violations of international humanitarian law committed by the enemy, NATO forces as well, and that this should be done on prescribed forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You also made an order on the 31st of March -- no, on the 29th of March, to rationalise the use of resources in carrying out combat assignments. What does that refer to, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since war was expected and the military industry had already been seriously damaged by then, I was issuing an order to rationally use ammunition, especially those calibres that were insufficient in the reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then there is an order issued on the 31st of March that has to do with the relocation of units from basic to reserve positions, or the relocation of units at the basic positions and reserve positions. That's what you signed.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In order to prevent losses from attacks, air attacks, every unit were supposed to have several areas, and after nightfall they were supposed to relocate to other positions so as not to suffer losses due to NATO airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must tell us the tab numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was tab 447. At the same time I wanted to say, Mr. Robinson, that you should admit into evidence those exhibits that I've already quoted from. Mr. Kwon said yesterday that when we finish this set of documents you should look at the exhibits involved. I've just completed a set of documents of this kind, so I ask that this be admitted into evidence, this set that I've dealt with now, in accordance with what Mr. Kwon said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You haven't dealt with tab 436 and 437, which will not be admitted, according to our practice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 436? Let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 436 is an order of yours, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You talk about taking measures to protect manpower and technical equipment and materiel.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a short telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the first sentence, it says: "A strong NATO attack is expected on our units in the area," and then you stipulate measures to protect your men. And in 437, a change in the area for the unit's base just before dusk. You explain that you changed the deployment of the unit to protect them from airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that is what those two tabs are about, Mr. Kwon. In order to save time, I thought I could gloss over them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Now, I'm going to ask you, Mr. Robinson, to agree, as you did last time, to having this set of documents from tab 448 to tab 469, that is to say 21 documents in all, go over this in express form, express procedure, because they relate to the Verification Mission in March. So just to indicate some of the characteristic features of the events that took place as expressed in the documents. So this is a set of documents, and they all relate to the Verification Mission for the entire month of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you have heard what has been said, that we should try and get through those tabs quickly. So as to not to have to discuss each one in turn, I'd just like to ask you to point out some of the characteristic features in those documents, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 448, for instance, that is the first document, and I should like to focus on point 3. On the 1st of March, following a report by someone, by an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. inhabitant, the OSCE mission with liaison officers toured the village of Gornje and Donje Ljubinje, the aim of which was to see whether the report was true that the army had occupied the school in the village and that there was no tuition in the school. On the spot in the school the teachers and representatives of the village said that, if necessary, at all times they would be happy to provide the army with accommodation, that it was their army. Then they said that tuition was following its normal course, that they didn't need the assistance of the mission to regulate relations with the army because that's something they could do themselves. The liaison officer said that his stay on the school premises was of a provisional character, and the representatives of the mission were not satisfied -- were satisfied that the previous report was proved wrong. So then another place was toured on the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, here we have a complaint by a farmer from the village, saying that some people stormed his house with socks over their heads, asking for cigarettes and brandy.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then -- well, he says that they were looking for brandy and cigarettes. All right. Now, General, let's --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is tab 451 that I'm looking at next, and there we have observations from a meeting and the questions that were asked by the mission or, rather, questions which were asked by the liaison officers where once again it is stated that Mr. Walker said that there were two streams, one which wanted to reach agreement and the other that did not, but they said that they knew -- they proposed daily contacts and believed that the army would never open fire first and launch provocations. But he says the Siptars always, through their mobile telephones, report things like this first of all, that is to say that the army was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He explained that. He said that the army would not engage in provocations but that they report the incidents and then the first people to get there would be proved right. That was the kind of principle they worked on.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then that same tab, towards the very end, it says: "He also said that one of the commanders of the KLA said that the KLA had decided to create a crisis and provoke the MUP and the army to react and that in less than five days something was bound to happen so as to create conditions for NATO intervention. And with respect to this Mr. Richard, and that was Mr. Ciaglinski that was referred to, said that the efforts of the OSCE mission were geared towards calming down the KLA and asked the army forces not allow themselves to be provoked and not to react to great strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you do your best not to be provoked and not to react too strongly?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the mission always observed that. That was their conclusion, that the army always did its best to avoid being provoked and that it even dealt with provocation -- was even too tolerant towards provocations. And on 452, page 2, it says under point 3 that the threats to the KLA that it would launch large-scale operations in novi Racak or Markale, of that type --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said that the verifiers always concluded that the army always did its best to avoid being provoked and that it even dealt or, rather, was even too tolerant towards provocations. Could you be more specific about that? Is that in this report or is that your own assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first part that you read out or mentioned, the former portion, was what the verifiers say. The latter was my response to the question put by Mr. Milosevic. That is to say whether we restrained ourselves from reacting. We restrained ourselves, held ourselves back too much, not to give cause for intervention on the part of NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought you said in response to Mr. Milosevic that the mission observed that the army was even too tolerant towards provocations. Is that what you intended to say, that the observers said that the army was too tolerant towards provocations, or is that simply your own assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my own assessment. Here is what the observers said: It says they proposed daily contacts and they believe that the army would never open fire first and launch provocations. But then it says the Siptars have mobile telephones and always manage to call up OSCE representatives first and say we're being attacked by the army and police. And since the mission does not know who opened fires first, it tends to believe the person who called up to report the incident first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is that? Where is that in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is tab 451, the fourth page, at the beginning, top of the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find it to make a note of it. I don't know whether Mr. Kay has found it, or Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 3, and it's the bottom paragraph there, if you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The end of page 3, and page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think so. No, Mr. Kay. Is this tab 451?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's just above paragraph 2, at the bottom there. Five lines above: "The Siptars have mobile phones..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So about ten lines up from the bottom on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the verifiers say that they are certain that the army would not open fire first. Does that mean and imply, since they say they're sure the army will not do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, when you start like that, that is -- that's going to end up as a leading question. You're telling the witness the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did the verifiers, in contacts with representatives of the army, assess the behaviour and conduct of our forces, of our army?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was a state institution, highly organised, had very proper relations with the verifiers, and they always stressed on the whole Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that they were satisfied with their relationship with the army, but they stressed, and we mentioned this last time, in February, speaking about February and throughout that time, they said what some of the problems that they encountered were between the OSCE and the army, but generally speaking, their relationships were proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, let's move on and get through this set of documents relating to the verifying mission. And it goes up to document 462.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 452, at the very beginning, as I've already said at that particular meeting at -- two KLA threats that they would launch large-scale operations, massive operations near Racak or Markale, of a New Racak or Markale, several sources have put out information that the terrorists have six huge explosive devices that they intend to use in an urban area, possibly in Pristina. And mention is made of two markets, two markets are being mentioned. The OSCE mission representatives said that everything would be done to prevent this from happening. So on the 4th of March, point 4, straight after that one it says that the verifiers spent time in the border belt, that they talked to the locals of the villages of Kusmin and Damjane and that they did not have any complaints, the residents had no complaints about the behaviour of the army, the VJ members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat, General, what tab that was.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said tab 452 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tab 452, top of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the top, yes. And the next passage I read out is point 4, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May we proceed, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to look at tab 454 now, please, point 4 of that tab. "Through conversations with OSCE mission representatives, we found out that the US policy towards Serbia regarding airstrikes had been partly altered, that is that there would be no rocket strikes even if a political agreement on Kosovo and Metohija was not signed. Strikes might be launched in case of a major incident or a major humanitarian disaster. There are indications that airstrikes should not be expected before the 15th of April, when NATO will be celebrating its 50th anniversary."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now tab 455 next. The 8th of March is the date. It is a meeting where the verifiers were present when the incident took place or, rather, when fire was opened at the army, when the army was fired at. But as they were present directly themselves, they had an office opened in Zur, they were able to verify this, the attack by the terrorists against the army, because they were personally present during that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have anything else that you would like to highlight as characteristic in the documents?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards the end. Once again touring the villages where the locals had no complaints with respect to the army's conduct. And I just wanted to highlight one more point. Once again an attack near the border on the 13th of March where a team of verifiers verified the attack on the army, which was there doing its regular duties in the region of the village of Zur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. May we proceed, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What number is that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is 461.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is becoming more like a local rather than an express train service.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. We are getting through these documents fairly quickly. The general has already reached tab 461. So we just have another eight documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything else characteristic there, General, in these next few documents?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In document 463, for instance, we have several incidents. On the 17th of March, that is to say three days before the mission left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija where they talked to the locals of the villages about their needs, the village of Vrbnica, they talked to the deputy leader and a member of the mission, Mr. Trevor confirmed that he had verified for himself that fire had been opened from their village on the army and that no army would have tolerated it. He advised them to stop such provocations of the army. He inquired -- he asked why the school was not working, and they said that it had not been working for just a few days, until Monday. And they asked -- when he asked them about any other problems they had, they asked the OSCE to provide them with a doctor and medicines. So that is to be found in tab 463.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do we have anything else?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now looking at tab 464, and the date of that is the 19th of March, and a meeting with General Drewienkiewicz where we learnt that at 1400 hours it was decided to evacuate the verification mission because the mission considered that to be necessary with respect to the extraordinary situation and in conformity with the decision at the mission between the OSCE and signed on the 16th. The OSCE is calling for cooperation with the MUP in pulling out. The MUP to provide security for the mission and its facilities and equipment. And as General Drewienkiewicz says, "We are leaving for a short while and we will be back." And he said that withdrawal will begin at 4.30 on the 20th of March. The next document is dated 19 March, tab 465. In the beginning, it says, that: "We have learned that OSCE verifiers in the field are carrying out their intelligence and reconnaissance activities by using original maps (WGS-84 from the M-709 series). Using them together with electronic and satellite photo transmitters, they locate features, facilities and the positions of forces, especially the army of Yugoslavia, in the LAB operations zone and on the general territory. In a situation that might be created, NATO forces would use the established positions for guidance and to bomb targets, that is VJ positions." Then in paragraph 3: "On the 18th of March, the head of Mission William Walker visited Skopje, where he met with the Supreme Allied Commander of the NATO forces Wesley Clark. According to Walker, the evaluations could be completed very quickly, if dislocation and moving out Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were to begin today, all of which will depend on the instructions from and the views taken at the headquarters of OSCE in Vienna." Then the next paragraph, the penultimate one, is this: "We have the information that Fernando del Mundo, an UNHCR official in Pristina, recorded an alleged humanitarian catastrophe, with numerical indicators, and forwarded the TV recordings to well-known international news agencies..." And there is one last report, that is one but last, tab 466, saying that in the course of the 20th of March planned relocation of the OSCE Verification Mission began at 0420 hours, that the mission was provided full security, and that no problems occurred during relocation. On the 21st of March we have another report saying that after departure of OSCE from the 20th onwards, about 200 to 300 members remained on the territory of Kosovo, including 30 to 50 officers "who will take on the role of forward air control officers and artillery reconnaissance, guiding and directing artillery fire. "According to our estimate, the marking of the targets and establishing of coordinates was mostly completed within the framework of verification tasks on KiM territory." In tab 468, towards the middle of the page, it says that with the help of the interpreter, who is still active, a message -- here it is: "Through the interpreter still working for the OSCE mission, the office of the federal government's commission received a message from General Drewienkiewicz that we should issue a denial on the telephone to the OSCE mission and General Drewienkiewicz that after their departure no humanitarian catastrophe had occurred on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija as Siptar extremists stubbornly insisted in numerous telephones calls and appeals for help. "They claimed that security forces had intensified combat operations against the Siptar population, that they were continuing to torch houses, that great numbers of people were moving out, that there were many civilian casualties, and that there was an exodus of the population. All this was calculated to bring about and force a NATO intervention. "All of this is clear to us in the mission; we just need your denial, said General Drewienkiewicz. "Our denial was sent to General Drewienkiewicz over my telephone, in direct contact with his official interpreter - Mrs. Marina." And the last tab, 469, is about the following: Humanitarian missions. The date is the 23rd of March. Humanitarian missions too left the territory of Yugoslavia using the border crossing Djeneral Jankovic, and Macedonia closed off the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. "A group of around 300 to 500 Siptar refugees who wished to go to Macedonia was held at the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned that mission members took down some coordinates on the map. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mission had global positioning system devices of the type called Magellan. I can speak about my specific zone. Only once did members of the mission enter my barracks directly and visit my office. My office was directly hit from the air. Only once did members of the mission visit the installation of Ceja [phoen] where they viewed tanks, took photos against the background of tanks, et cetera. This installation Ceja was hit during the first airstrike and after that it was bombed another 700 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, General. Did members of the Verification Mission collect intelligence on our forces and their deployment in order to prepare the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak of all members of the mission, and I cannot tell you now which of them did and which didn't, because certainly there was a great number of them who did their work in all honesty. But there were also some members of the mission that did collect intelligence on our forces. And at the end of the day I can give you specific examples, a number of them, showing direct communication between members of the mission through satellite telephones with KLA commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have data about this, you say.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is my personal experience, and I was there on the spot. So, yes, it is the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I would now like you to admit these exhibits, ending with 469 inclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit them. I'm not sure if all of them are translated. If there are any that are not translated, then those will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you issued an order on the 2nd of April that relates to the adoption of certain measures to protect personnel in your area of deployment. That's tab 470. What is it about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, give us an estimate now as to when you will conclude your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope it will be today, Mr. Robinson. I'm really trying to go as fast as I can. There are very many documents. During the preparation of this witness we used 10.000 documents, which means that I'm presenting only 6 per cent of this amount through these binders. But it is necessary to see the conduct of the army, how it operated. You see that we are going through events which are very pertinent, because they are referred to in a completely different light both in the indictment and in witness statements and testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This order was based on an oral order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's 10.30, and I have a meeting now. We'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in document 471, we have an order to smash and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the Jablanica sector. Could we go through it quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Jablanica sector is to the north-west of Djakovica. This territory, too, held a large concentration of Siptar terrorist forces Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. precisely on the axis that emerges towards Junik and the block house of Kosare and where some of the fiercest fighting during the war took place. So this is an order of the superior command to crush and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the Jablanica sector. It was sent to all units of the corps that were to be involved. This is the traditional type of order specifying the assignments for all the brigades. The assignment for my brigade was to act from Crmljane and Raskoc and to support MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, it says: "Escort captured terrorists to the prison for prisoner of war collection centres." And: "Prohibit the uncontrolled entry of unit members into populated areas, looting of property and military equipment belonging to the enemy, the robbing of bodies and entering into enemy shelters prior to the arrival of the specialist organs."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just as in previous orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything particular that we should dwell on here?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then in document 474 we have a map showing the 125th Brigade and 252nd Motorised Brigade and the 549th Motorised Brigade, which is yours.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along with this order of the superior command, this map is given which indicates in graphic terms the assignments of various units, including my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And in tab 473 we have another map. What does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also a map from the superior command. It pertains to the assignment that has already been given but it also pertains to the control of the territory where the forces of the terrorists had already been crushed, that is the Malisevo sector in particular. This came down from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In document 474, you made a report that describes the situation in your area of responsibility, and you sent this to the command of the Pristina Corps. Could you please dwell on it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my report to the corps command about what is going on in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning you say, in line 3, a particular problem is the large number of refugees.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is line 3 in tab 474.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then you go on to say how many refugees there are. You say the very incidence of refugees, especially in that number, came as a surprise. "The position of the authorities in the first days was not to allow the refugees to leave the country but for everybody to return instead to their homes; however, that was not feasible, because the refugees were coming in ever greater numbers from the remotest parts of Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say: "In those first days from the 24th to the 31st, the refugees were allowed to enter Albania unhindered, whereafter they were refused entry first into the Republic of Macedonia and then into Albania as well." Was it our authorities that prohibited them from entering Macedonia or -- and Albania or theirs?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the Albanian authorities and Macedonian authorities. Something was going on at the border so that for two or three days they couldn't cross over. And after entry was finally allowed, the flow of refugees was slowed down. We noticed that a registration process had begun, and that was what slowed them down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Here in this report you said that the position of the authorities in those first days was not to allow the refugees to leave the country. Have you seen this kind of document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It says here, by the way, that I found this out in my contacts with the MUP, with the head of the Secretariat of Internal Affairs, who was my counterpart on this territory. He was in command of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it says not to allow the refugees to leave the country but instead to return into their homes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it says it was not feasible because the refugees were coming in ever greater numbers from the remotest parts of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my explanation would be this: If all the refugees had been stopped and if nobody else would be coming in, we would have been able to deal with the current column, but they were coming in from all directions. There were alternate routes, for instance from Prizren or the road between Prizren and Djakovica, and they were constantly coming in by that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to describe what you concluded from your talks with the refugees. You say: "Based on the talks we had with individuals in the columns of refugees, the following conclusions can be made as to their reasons for leaving our territory:" And then you say: "a) Fear of major fighting that is expected to follow between our forces, on the one hand, and the KLA and NATO forces on the other."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "They are saying that fighting will probably take place everywhere on our territory, with great intensity, and that they will have nowhere to hide. In response to our offer to go to Serbia, they say it is realistic to expect a less than warm welcome there because it is their fellow countrymen who had caused the war."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then goes paragraph b): "A certain number of Siptars say that they are leaving the country to avoid forced mobilisation into KLA ranks and that it is current practice for every family to send a certain number of its members to the KLA or, alternatively, to pay a large amount of money."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the practice in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph c): "A large number of refugees say that they fear the army and the police, and they are particularly afraid of 'Arkan's troops.' Asked whether they have seen any 'Arkan's troops,' none were able to confirm, saying only that they had heard about them from others. This is probably KLA's psychological propaganda, aimed at getting as many of the populace as possible to leave." That is your estimate. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Then you go on to say: "Asked whether they fear us, the army, and whether we have ever done anything to harm them, everyone promptly replies that they do not fear the army and that it is their army and they would stay if only there were army troops where they lived."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "However, despite these statements, we believed -- we believe their fear of the army and police is justified since many families had members in the KLA and were therefore afraid of how we might react when we learn about it. "d) Fear of NATO bombing was emphasised by all groups as the primary reason, because in their words they do not distinguish between troops and civilians and do not look where they are striking." And then you say most of them have enough food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are reading from the document, and the interpreter is asking you to do that more slowly. In any event, it is time for you to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you say that all of these are reasons that you established on the basis of conversations with refugees from these columns.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to them several times, not only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally talk to them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I myself talked to them. And on several occasions I even helped some individuals or groups of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say here: "d) That fear of NATO bombing was emphasised by all groups as the primary reason, because in their words they do not distinguish between troops and civilians and do not look where they are striking." Is that what they told you personally?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they told me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We've already dealt with the other reasons, and now you say on page 2, at the beginning of page 2, so I'm going to ask you about what the attitude of the police and the army was towards persons in these columns.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that on the whole it was correct, proper. However, our officers stated that a small number of MUP members and a small number of army members tried to take property away from refugees, primarily money or vehicles. All these cases that were reported to us by MUP patrols or military police patrols were resolved. So eight persons, that is to say two privates and six conscripts, were disciplined, and criminal reports were filed against another six conscripts who were arrested. They were members of my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, for this interview, do you remember how many Albanians you met at that time? Your report is based on how many interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Albanians -- these were endless columns. I did not talk to them only on one day but at different localities, on the road between Prizren and Djakovica. I talked to them about ten times. Sometimes I would stop with my vehicle because I would see, for instance - that was on three occasions - that vehicles belonging to these Albanians had broken down and that they were standing by the road. I stopped to ask them why they had stopped, what the problem was. On two occasions these were tractors. Their tyres had a problem and they couldn't resolve them. I said that they could freely use the abandoned tractors on the roads. There were a great many of those, because there was something wrong with those tractors, and I said that they could take off their tyres and continue their journey. And I asked them where they were from and why they were going to Albania. The third time, I helped a man. His engine had broken down. It was no longer working. I talked to him. He had a rather numerous family, and I asked him how I could help him. He said, "Well, you can help me if you would stop a vehicle and order them to trail me to Albania." I waited for the first vehicle that I thought could do that. I stopped that vehicle, and I asked the driver, the owner, whether he'd want to help this man, and he said, "By all means. There's no problem. I want to help him." So he attached the vehicle that had broken down to his own and that's how they continued their journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. This report is a result of your personal contacts with the refugees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking how many refugees there were on that road? There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. I'm asking how many interviews did you have with the refugees. You said about ten times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About ten times I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you say here further on towards the end that what is interesting are the views of the bodies of local self-administration on the reasons why Siptars are leaving for Albania. "In addition to the reasons we have stated, they also underline the following: "1. They are leaving the country in line with the pre-arranged scenario of a 'humanitarian catastrophe' in order to justify the bombing and the aggression. "2. They are leaving and abandoning the territory so that the 'NATO alliance' could bomb all targets indiscriminately in the future, with only Serbs and their supporters remaining in Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the view of the local administration, of the Serbs for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you find it persuasive at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already mentioned my own reasons, but their reasons were of interest too. That's why I put them down here. Certainly today, after all this time, I believe that there was a prepared scenario.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, may I ask, what prompted you to carry out these interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, I know that there are refugees in every war, but there were many refugees. These columns were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. endless. I saw that there were refugees from other places too.
